issues.description: Attribute/Getter name mismatch for ExcellenceLand.boolean attribute: The UML in the problem statement names the boolean attribute 'excellentEnough' (ExcellenceLand: -excellentEnough: boolean) and instructs students to provide getters for all attributes. The solution implementation, however, uses a different attribute name 'isExcellent' and provides a getter isExcellent(). This deviates from the UML/requirements and results in a public API that does not match the specification (students following the UML would implement getExcellentEnough()/isExcellentEnough(), while the solution exposes isExcellent()). This inconsistency can confuse students about the exact attribute name and expected getter name and may cause automated checks to fail if they expect the UML-based names.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the solution match the UML and problem description: rename the boolean attribute in ExcellenceLand to 'excellentEnough' and provide a corresponding getter (either isExcellentEnough() or getExcellentEnough(), consistent with Java boolean getter conventions). Also ensure the constructor parameter name matches (e.g. ExcellenceLand(double excellencyLevel, boolean excellentEnough, List<Ride> rides)). Alternatively, update the problem statement/UML to use 'isExcellent' if that name is preferred, so all artifacts share the same attribute name and getter.

issues.description: The UML in the problem statement defines a boolean attribute named 'excellentEnough' for ExcellenceLand, but the solution implementation names the boolean field 'isExcellent' (with getter isExcellent()). This is a naming mismatch for the same conceptual attribute (whether the park is excellent enough) and can confuse students when they try to map the UML-specified attribute to the implementation/constructor/getter names.
issues.suggested_fix: Align the identifier across artifacts. Either rename the boolean field and getter in the implementation to match the UML ('excellentEnough' with getter isExcellentEnough() or getExcellentEnough()), or update the UML/problem statement to use 'isExcellent' if that name is preferred. Prefer matching the UML to avoid student confusion.
